title: Standard Test Method ASTM D 7998-19 for the Cohesive Strength Development of Wood Adhesives
protocol: Use a sliced veneer of about 0.6 to 0.8 mm thick from a reliable producer.
Cut the veneer sheets into 305 mm squares.
Condition the wood at 21 °C and 50% relative humidity for at least a day.
Select hard maple (Acer saccharum) face veneers for their surface smoothness.
Ensure the veneers are free from defects such as discoloration and uneven surfaces.
Place a piece of veneer under the cutting blades so that the grain is parallel with the long direction.
Depress the air pressure button to cut each wood piece to 20 mm by 117 mm.
Move the veneer under the cutting blades to an uncut area and depress the button again to cut another piece.
Continue cutting until the piece of veneer is completely cut into pieces.
Clean the platens of any adhesive residue from previous samples.
Adjust the temperature of the platens to the desired setting and allow them to equilibrate.
Operate the equipment in a room at 21 °C and 50% RH for bonding wood specimens.
If operating conditions do not meet 21 °C and 50% RH, keep conditioned specimens in a plastic bag until bonding.
Design the method to collect kinetic cure data accurately as outlined in ASTM D7998-1911.
Spread 5 mg of adhesive over the terminal 0.5 cm of the wood specimen sufficiently to cover the bonding area.
Transfer the adhesive to the other specimen without excessive squeeze out.
Tare the wood specimen on a balance and re-weigh after adhesive application to ensure consistent spread rate.
Exercise great care in distributing the adhesive evenly.
Overlap the specimens and ensure they are aligned properly.
Use a spatula method for applying adhesive to achieve an even distribution.
Use a microbalance to measure the amount of adhesive applied accurately.
Bond the specimens at 120 °C for 2 min and condition them overnight at 21 °C and 50% RH.
Lock a sample in place by closing the grips on the ABES tester, ensuring proper alignment.
Press the start button on the machine to activate the platens, pressing on the overlapped section of the specimen at 120 °C for 2 min.
Retract the platens and loosen the grips after bonding.
Remove the samples from the ABES tester.
Lock a sample in place by closing the grips on the ABES tester ensuring alignment with the tester.
Press the start button to initiate pulling through a servodrive while one end pulls on a load cell attached to the grips.
Continue pulling until the bond breaks, recording the maximum force as bond strength.
Use the same procedure for dry and water-soaked samples.
Ensure tight grip holding of the wood to avoid slipping during testing.
Discard values if the sample breaks outside the bonded area.
Determine the rate of strength development by varying temperature and time.
Begin testing at 100 °C platen temperature with bonding times ranging from 10 to 210 seconds in increments of 30 seconds.
Raise the temperature by 10 °C after completing all times at each previous temperature.
Repeat bonding tests until no linear section remains for strength versus time at low bonding times.
Retract the platens after bonding.
Use the air cooling feature of the ABES to cool the sample to near room temperature.
Measure the sample strength once cooled.
Start with a low pressing time and increase for subsequent samples.
Collect strength versus time data until increasing time results in little or no increase in strength.
Repeat the sequence at higher temperatures to yield the plot of strength versus time.
Regress isothermal strength development rate versus temperature.
Cool the sample before testing for isothermal strength development.
Heat the platens to a specified temperature, such as 220 °C.
Close the platens onto the pre-bonded sample for 2 minutes at the specified temperature.
Measure the bond strength after opening the platens.
Determine any thermal softening of the adhesive compared to the bonding temperature of 120°C.
Close the platens on the sample for 30 minutes.
Test the sample for strength after heating to determine its heat resistance.
Release the platens and test the sample's strength again to compare with pre-heating values.
Use rapid heating in ABES to measure strength while hot without moving the sample.
Differentiate between thermal softening and chemical degradation based on the results.
Analyze images of the failed bonding surface.
